While originally identified as a genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), TREM2 functions as a context-dependent immunometabolic checkpoint rather than a uniform phenotypic driver, exerting divergent biological outputs dictated by distinct tissue microenvironments and ligand repertoires. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of TREM2 immunobiology, detailing how ligand engagement-including cell-surface phospholipids and apolipoprotein E (ApoE)-activates the DAP12/DAP10-SYK-PI3K-mTOR signalling axis. This coordinated intracellular cascade instructively drives myeloid adaptation towards metabolically competent disease-associated microglia (DAM) and lipid-associated macrophage (LAM) states, sustaining bioenergetics and debris clearance under pathological stress. Across neurodegenerative proteinopathies and acute cerebral ischemia, TREM2 signalling is predominantly neuroprotective by promoting aggregate compaction and mitigating secondary excitotoxicity, although chronic dysregulated activation may drive stage-dependent neuroinflammation. In peripheral inflammatory pathologies such as rheumatoid arthritis and sepsis, TREM2 fine-tunes macrophage efferocytosis and systemic metabolic thresholds. In oncology, TREM2 displays a complex, microenvironment-dependent divergence: in central nervous system malignancies such as glioblastoma (GBM), TREM2 exerts controversial, stage-dependent effects, spanning microglial tumour containment in early stages versus pro-tumoural myelin recycling and immunosuppression by monocyte-derived macrophages in post-treatment recurrence; conversely, in peripheral solid tumours, monocyte-derived TREM2+ tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) predominantly orchestrate an immunosuppressive, nutrient-deprived niche that impairs cytotoxic T-cell function. Furthermore, we synthesise emerging paradigms along the bidirectional microbiome-gut-brain-tumour axis, elucidating how commensal and intra-tumoural microbial cues dynamically calibrate myeloid signalling tone and therapeutic susceptibility. We address translation bottlenecks-including blood-brain barrier (BBB) shuttles, human trial scarcity and soluble TREM2 (sTREM2) biomarker harmonisation-outlining a biomarker-guided, context-tailored precision therapeutic framework for targeting the TREM2 axis.

title: Freezing of Gait: A Therapeutic Perspective.
abstract: Despite improved definition of the problem and better understanding of its phenomenology, freezing of gait (FoG) remains a therapeutic enigma for clinicians and neuroscientists alike. Patients with Parkinson disease (PD) or other neurological disorders experiencing FoG are similarly frustrated, despite the benefits that levodopa and other medications provide for control of PD's primary motor features. For those burdened by episodes of FoG, current therapeutic options are quite limited. Some patients achieve improvements from pharmacotherapy-for example, by adjunctive use of an oral dopaminergic agonist or by subcutaneous infusion of apomorphine. If needed, deep brain stimulation sometimes offers symptomatic improvements. Certain interventions devised by physical therapists (or discovered by patients themselves) can improve FoG. However, successful pharmacotherapy for FoG has lagged behind, though the future holds some promising leads for therapies acting on dopaminergic, adenosinergic, noradrenergic, glutamatergic, and cholinergic circuitry.

title: State of the "Art" in Freezing of Gait: Drawing on Perspectives of Individuals With Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) in Parkinson's disease (PD) is increasingly recognized as a multidimensional phenomenon encompassing motor, cognitive, and emotional domains. The impact of FoG is enormous, but can be difficult to articulate. Traditional clinical assessments typically fail to capture its subjective and affective impact. This qualitative study explored drawings from individuals with PD to better understand the lived experience of FoG. Specifically, we collected artworks created by individuals who experience FoG. We studied the personal perceptions and emotions associated with FoG drawings in two ways: by asking participants to narratively explain their artwork and a qualitative curation by an international panel of experts of neurology, neuroscience, neurorehabilitation, neuroaesthetics, art, and empirical aesthetics. Five overarching themes emerged: (1) "Captured feet," depicting sensations of being glued, tethered, or rooted to the ground; (2) "Chaos," reflecting disrupted motor control during environmental or cognitive overload; (3) "Emotional explosion," expressing fear, anger, helplessness, and loss of control; (4) "Freezing and falls," highlighting instability and existential threat; and (5) "Released from freeze," portraying therapeutic relief, restored movement, and joy. These visual narratives reveal that FoG is more than just a motor block. Rather, it is an embodied experience of immobilization, emotional escalation, and vulnerability, contrasted by profound relief when mobility returns. Artistic expression offers unique insights beyond structured assessments, fostering empathetic clinician-patient communication, and supporting a more holistic, person-centered approach to PD care.

title: Consistency of Serial Cerebrospinal Fluid α-Synuclein Seed Amplification Assay Results in the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: Studies reporting α-synuclein seed amplification assay (aSyn-SAA) results are often cross-sectional. In this study, we investigated the intraindividual consistency of aSyn-SAA results (Amprion) over time from participants in the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI). A total of 1238 participants had >1 cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) aSyn-SAA result for analysis (Parkinson's disease [PD] = 633, prodromal = 563, healthy control [HC] = 42), collected over a median (minimum, maximum) of 2.0 (0.4, 11.4) years. Emphasis was placed on evaluating consistency in aSyn-SAA-PD participants, aSyn-SAA + HC participants, and conversion rates from aSyn-SAA negative to positive results prodromal participants. Of aSyn-SAA + PD participants, 96% (474/493, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 94%-98%) remained positive in subsequent samples, and 92% (116/126, 95% CI: 86%-96%) of aSyn-SAA-PD participants remained negative. Ninety-nine percent (303/307, 95% CI: 97%-99%) of aSyn-SAA + prodromal participants remained positive, and 95% (234/247, 95% CI: 91%-97%) of aSyn-SAA-prodromal participants remained negative. Eighty-nine percent (16/18, 95% CI: 67%-97%) of aSyn-SAA + HC participants remained positive, and 87% (20/23, 95% CI: 68%-95%) of aSyn-SAA-HC participants remained negative. aSyn-SAA testing is highly consistent over time, even in less expected scenarios. © 2026 The Author(s). Movement Disorders published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title: Juvenile Huntington Disease With Cerebellar-Predominant Atrophy Identified by Genome Sequencing.
journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology
abstract: Juvenile Huntington disease accounts for a small fraction of Huntington disease cases and is driven by the largest trinucleotide repeat expansions. We describe a 6-year-old boy with progressive global regression, generalized dystonia, and epilepsy, in whom serial imaging showed striking cerebellar-predominant atrophy with an initially normal-appearing striatum. Extensive metabolic testing, exome sequencing, and an ataxia repeat expansion panel were nondiagnostic. Research genome sequencing identified a large pathogenic huntingtin CAG repeat expansion that confirmatory testing sized beyond 180 repeats. This case illustrates a cerebellar-predominant imaging signature of extreme repeat expansions and the limitations of exome sequencing for detecting them.

title: The Neural Symphony in the Periodontium: Health, Inflammation, and Regeneration.
abstract: Periodontal nerves, comprising sensory, sympathetic, and parasympathetic fibers, are essential components of the periodontium. Beyond their classic sensory and proprioceptive functions, these neural networks actively modulate periodontal immune responses, bone remodeling, and tissue regeneration. They orchestrate tissue homeostasis by releasing specific neuropeptides, neurotransmitters, and neurotrophic factors. The progression of periodontitis is intimately linked to neural dysregulation, where proinflammatory mediators (e.g., excessive substance P and sympathetic catecholamines) overpower protective signals (e.g., calcitonin gene-related peptide and parasympathetic acetylcholine). Conversely, successful periodontal regeneration requires the restoration of this neural equilibrium. Nerve terminals rapidly sprout into osteogenic zones during early repair. Subsequently, their spatiotemporally patterned signaling suppresses osteoclastogenesis and promotes the osteogenic differentiation of stem cells. Crucially, these local neural networks function as a bidirectional conduit linking the periodontium to the central nervous system: systemic stressors (eg, sleep deprivation and chronic stress) can compromise ganglionic autophagy or trigeminal function to exacerbate periodontal bone loss, while periodontal pathogens can reciprocally exploit these pathways to induce central neuroinflammation. Recognizing this interconnected oral-neural-brain axis not only explains why certain periodontitis-susceptible patients remain refractory to conventional therapies but also highlights the broader impact of periodontal inflammation on neurodegenerative risk. Furthermore, nerve-targeted strategies, including neurotrophin-functionalized biomaterials, local neuropeptide delivery, and bioelectric neuromodulation, offer promising approaches to resolving refractory inflammation, restoring periodontal integrity, and concurrently mitigating the risk of associated central neuroinflammation. In this review, we comprehensively characterize the spatiotemporal plasticity of periodontal nerves under physiological and pathological conditions. We dissect the molecular mechanisms linking neural signaling to periodontal immunity and repair, and highlight how integrating neurobiology into periodontology could advance the development of next-generation regenerative medicine.

title: Preoperative Functional Imaging Predicts Deep Brain Stimulation Outcome in Craniocervical Dystonia.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established treatment for craniocervical dystonia (CCD), yet postoperative benefit varies widely and cannot be estimated before surgery. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has shown prognostic value across DBS indications. The objective of this study was to develop and externally validate preoperative rs-fMRI models estimating DBS response in CCD. Forty-two patients from two independent centers underwent preoperative 3 T rs-fMRI (discovery, n = 26; validation, n = 16). Using 12 literature-informed, symptom-relevant regions of interest, we quantified the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation as a measure of intrinsic regional neural activity. We applied regularized modeling to classify super-responders, distinguish responders from non-responders, and estimate improvement in Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale motor subscore. When applied to the validation cohort, the imaging models achieved a three-category classification accuracy of 75.0% (50.5%-89.8%) using a sequential two-step procedure (Pperm = 0.002). Predicted continuous improvement was also correlated with empirical improvement (Rext = 0.65, Q2 = 0.34, Pperm = 0.004). Within the discovery cohort, nested leave-one-out-cross-validation, in which feature selection and decision-threshold derivation were repeated independently within each training fold, yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.73 (0.50-0.96) and 0.77 (0.51-1.00). Across models, baseline primary motor cortex activity was consistently associated with diminished postoperative benefit. Preoperative rs-fMRI captures clinically relevant variation in baseline brain state in CCD, with predictive performance supported in an external validation. These findings provide preliminary support for rs-fMRI as a potential source of information to aid patient counseling and clinical decision-making, pending prospective validation. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title: Assessing the use of ASAP-MS for Screening a UK Pub for Illicit Drug Substances.
abstract: Illicit drug use in social environments, such as pubs and bars, has become an increasingly significant issue for public health and safety. These venues often provide a setting where individuals may engage in recreational drug use, resulting in their residual presence on high-contact surfaces. This study aims to investigate the presence of illicit drugs in a pub within the United Kingdom, focusing on common touchpoints such as the tables, bar and men's/women's bathrooms. Over 400 surface swabs were collected across 3 weeks, with the objective of identifying traces of illicit substances commonly associated with recreational use. This study additionally explored the potential of atmospheric solids analysis probe mass spectrometry (ASAP-MS) as a screening tool for the on-site detection of cocaine, ketamine, amphetamine, diazepam and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). Previous research has demonstrated that ASAP-MS is an effective method for detecting illicit drugs with minimal sample preparation. An untargeted screening method was developed for direct swab analysis via glass capillary rod, whereas a combined untargeted and targeted approach was used for solvent-extracted samples. For confirmatory testing, liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS) determined the effectiveness of each ASAP-MS analysis. Results indicated that the targeted method with minimal sample preparation detected trace amounts of illicit drugs that were previously undetected using the initial screening method. However, the untargeted method, with direct sample analysis, showed potential for detecting larger quantities, particularly cocaine. Overall, the findings revealed drug residues at all touchpoints within the pub, particularly in the bathrooms which contained traces of cocaine in all samples.

title: Unraveling Shared Molecular Mechanisms in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Neuropathic Pain: Targeting p38 MAPK and Wnt/β-Catenin Pathways.
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Parkinson's Disease (PD), and Neuropathic Pain (NP), share overlapping molecular and cellular mechanisms that contribute to progressive neuronal dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and impaired neural repair. Although these conditions present with distinct clinical manifestations, accumulating evidence indicates that dysregulation of the p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK) and Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathways represents a common pathogenic axis underlying disease initiation and progression. Activation of p38 MAPK amplifies inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuronal apoptosis, and glial activation, whereas suppression of Wnt/β-catenin signaling disrupts synaptic plasticity, blood-brain barrier integrity, neurogenesis, and neuronal survival. The reciprocal interaction between these pathways further exacerbates amyloid-β accumulation, dopaminergic neuronal degeneration, tau hyperphosphorylation, central sensitization, and persistent neuroimmune activation, thereby linking cognitive decline, motor impairment, and chronic pain. This review comprehensively examines the molecular crosstalk between p38 MAPK and Wnt/β-catenin signaling across AD, PD, and NP, highlighting their roles in regulating neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial homeostasis, and neuronal resilience. In addition, it summarizes emerging pharmacological agents, natural bioactive compounds, and targeted therapeutic strategies designed to inhibit p38 MAPK activation or restore Wnt/β-catenin signaling to promote neuroprotection and functional recovery. Particular emphasis is placed on the translational potential of dual-pathway modulation as a disease-modifying approach that addresses shared pathological mechanisms rather than isolated disease- specific manifestations. By integrating current experimental and clinical evidence, this review provides a unified mechanistic perspective, identifies promising therapeutic opportunities for developing more effective interventions against neurodegenerative disorders and neuropathic pain, and outlines the remaining challenges for future translational research.

title: Protective Effects of Phenytoin and Spironolactone against 5-Fluorouracil-induced Alopecia: Involvement of Antioxidant, Anti-inflammatory, and Collagen-regenerative Mechanisms.
journal: Anti-inflammatory & anti-allergy agents in medicinal chemistry
abstract: Chemotherapy-induced alopecia (CIA) is one of the most distressing adverse effects of cancer treatment and is primarily associated with oxidative stress, inflammation, and damage to hair follicles. Effective preventive and therapeutic options remain limited. This study evaluated the protective effects of oral phenytoin and spironolactone against 5-fluorouracil (5-FU)- induced alopecia in rats. CIA was induced in rats using intraperitoneal administration of 5-FU, followed by daily oral treatment with phenytoin or spironolactone for 21 days. Feed intake, body weight, and hair regrowth were monitored throughout the study. Blood and skin samples were collected for assessment of oxidative stress markers, inflammatory cytokines, and histological changes using Haematoxylin and Eosin and Von Gieson staining. 5-FU administration significantly reduced feed intake and body weight and induced marked alopecia, impaired hair regrowth, and follicular degeneration. Treatment with phenytoin and spironolactone improved appetite, attenuated weight loss, and enhanced hair regrowth. Both agents significantly reduced oxidative stress, as evidenced by decreased plasma malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, lowered TNF-α and IL-1β concentrations, and restored IL-10 levels. Histological analyses revealed that 5-FU caused dermal papilla distortion, follicular shrinkage, loss of anagen follicles, and disruption of collagen organization. These alterations were markedly ameliorated by both treatments, with improved follicular architecture, hair shaft integrity, collagen organization, and anagen activity. Phenytoin produced greater improvements in selected hair morphometric indices. The findings indicate that attenuation of oxidative stress and inflammation was accompanied by improved follicular structure and hair regrowth, suggesting that these mechanisms may contribute to the protective effects of both agents. The greater improvement in selected morphometric indices with phenytoin indicates potentially differential effects on follicular recovery. Phenytoin and spironolactone effectively attenuated 5-FU-induced alopecia, oxidative stress, inflammation, and follicular damage. Their protective effects suggest potential therapeutic utility in promoting post-chemotherapy hair recovery and improving treatment outcomes.

title: The Role and Mechanisms of Gut Microbiota in the Progression of Hepatic Encephalopathy.
abstract: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a severe complication of end-stage liver disease that is associated with high mortality; however, its therapeutic options remain limited. The traditional mechanistic understanding focuses on ammonia neurotoxicity, although intestinal bacteria also play a significant role through the gut-liver-brain axis. This review primarily discusses the characteristics of gut dysbiosis in HE, which is marked by a progressive loss of beneficial commensals (e.g., Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae, and Faecalibacterium) and an overgrowth of potentially pathogenic bacteria (e.g., Enterobacteriaceae, Streptococcaceae, and Veillonellaceae). Unlike previous reviews which have largely focused on phylum- or genus-level changes, this review provides a species-level synthesis of gut microbial alterations in HE. We further summarise the multifaceted mechanisms by which the gut microbiota contributes to HE pathogenesis, including the impairment of intestinal barrier integrity, activation of systemic and neuroinflammation, alterations in microbial metabolites (such as ammonia, short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and aromatic amino acids), and disruption of neuroendocrine signalling pathways. Furthermore, herein we summarise the microbiota-targeted intervention measures for HE, including aetiological treatments, drug therapies (lactulose and rifaximin), live microbial therapies (probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, faecal microbiota transplantation, etc.), and dietary adjustments. Emerging approaches, such as engineered bacteria and phage therapy, are also discussed, along with the barriers to their clinical translation and safety considerations. In summary, targeting the gut microbiota offers a new approach for the precise treatment of HE, although challenges remain in translating these findings into routine clinical practice.

title: miR-124 delivery to the hippocampus reduces excitability, enhances neurogenesis and affects microglia in a model of Alzheimer's disease.
journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
abstract: MicroRNA-124 (miR-124) has been proposed as therapeutic candidate for Alzheimer's disease (AD), given its regulation of gene networks governing synaptic function, neurogenesis and inflammation. However, its functional role during early disease stages, and the cellular context-dependence of its effects, remain unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of targeted neuronal miR-124 delivery to the hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) of AppNL-G-F mice. At an earlier 'presymptomatic' stage, miR-124 reduced intrinsic excitability of mature granule neurons and induced subtle changes in dendritic architecture. Integrative transcriptomic analyses revealed that predicted miR-124 targets were enriched among downregulated genes involved in synapse organization and cell junction assembly. At the same time, miR-124 increased the number of immature neurons and microglia, indicating structural and functional remodeling of the DG. At a later 'symptomatic' disease stage, where AD pathology is established, neuronal miR-124 supplementation reduced DG Aβ40 and Aβ42 levels and decreased local amyloid plaque burden, while also altering the plaque-associated microglial response. Together, these findings identify neuronal miR-124 as a context- and disease-stage-dependent regulator of the DG microenvironment and demonstrate effects extending from neuronal function to other cellular populations and local AD-associated pathology.

title: Melatonin Suppresses Colorectal Cancer Alongside Coordinated Changes in H3K4me3Q5ser and m6A Modifications.
abstract: Melatonin has demonstrated antitumor activity in various cancer models, but its effects may depend on the therapeutic dose and cellular environment. We found that melatonin at millimolar concentrations significantly downregulated transglutaminase 2 (TGM2), histone serotonylation (H3K4me3Q5ser), and YTHDF1/m6A (N6-methyladenosine) in a colorectal cancer model. Cross-interference between TGM2 and YTHDF1 supports a link between these regulatory processes, while molecular docking, pharmacological interventions, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments suggest the existence of a signaling pathway involving melatonin and the HTR2B receptor. A combined analysis of CHIP-seq and meRIP-seq identified salt-induced kinase 1 (SIK1) as a potential downstream target, and SIK1 interference affected the proliferation and migration of colorectal cancer. Collectively, these findings support a working model in which melatonin-induced tumor suppression is associated with coordinated changes in TGM2/H3K4me3Q5ser and YTHDF1-associated m6A regulation, with SIK1 emerging as a potential convergent downstream effector.

title: Temporal dynamics of the cerebrospinal fluid proteome in tick-borne encephalitis and enteroviral meningitis.
abstract: Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) is a severe viral infection of the central nervous system (CNS), causing acute meningoencephalitis and often long-term neurocognitive sequelae. The lack of specific treatment for TBE highlights the need to improve understanding of disease mechanisms and identify novel biomarkers. Enteroviral meningitis is typically a milder infection of the CNS and rarely causes encephalitis. In this hypothesis-generating study, we aimed to characterise temporal changes in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteome in TBE and identify candidate biomarkers associated with pathophysiological mechanisms, disease severity, and neurocognitive outcome. Patients with TBE, enteroviral meningitis, or aseptic meningoencephalitis of unknown origin were retrospectively included from a previously established cohort. CSF proteomes were analysed by label-free mass spectrometry, followed by differential protein expression analysis and functional annotation. Temporal proteome dynamics and protein associations with disease severity and neurocognitive outcome were assessed. Data are available via ProteomeXchange with identifier PXD077931. Proteomic analyses revealed alterations in proteins related to synaptic function, inflammatory pathways, the complement system, and the 14-3-3 protein family. Adrenomedullin was markedly increased in the late phase of TBE compared with enteroviral meningitis. Temporal changes in the CSF proteome in TBE indicate a strong inflammatory response occurring in concert with lower levels of proteins related to synaptic function during the acute phase. These findings provide insights into the host response and pathogenesis of TBE and identify proteins of potential interest for future validation.

title: How well do junior neurology residents recognize multiple sclerosis? Analysis of the "Close the Loop" resident clinical acumen project.
abstract: To evaluate diagnostic accuracy and patterns of errors among junior neurology residents evaluating acute presentations of multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating diseases. We retrospectively reviewed a morning-report case log of overnight neurology consultations presented by postgraduate year-2 residents at a New York academic center over 6 years. Cases with an initial resident impression of multiple sclerosis/demyelinating disease or a final diagnosis of multiple sclerosis/demyelinating disease were analyzed using a predefined localization-etiology schema. Among 1301 cases with uncertain initial diagnoses, 66 (5.1%) had an initial resident impression of multiple sclerosis/demyelinating disease and 57 (4.4%) had a final multiple sclerosis/demyelinating disease diagnosis. Overall diagnostic accuracy for multiple sclerosis/demyelinating disease presentations was 66.7%. Of initial multiple sclerosis/demyelinating disease impressions, 33.3% were incorrect (over-called); most errors occurred at the level of neurologic versus non-neurologic (40.9%) and central nervous system etiologies (40.9%). Among confirmed multiple sclerosis/demyelinating disease cases, 22.8% were under-called, predominantly due to errors in central nervous system etiology (69.2%). Acute multiple sclerosis/demyelinating disease presentations pose educational challenges for neurology residents, with errors primarily arising from misclassification of central nervous system etiologies. Diagnostic accuracy was influenced by prior disease history and patient age, highlighting cognitive biases such as framing and anchoring. Structured feedback models like "close the loop" may help improve multiple sclerosis diagnostic acumen in residency training and clinical practice.

title: Intraoperative Anesthetic Parameters Predict Early Allograft Dysfunction in Pediatric Living Donor Liver Transplantation.
abstract: Early allograft dysfunction (EAD) is a major complication of pediatric liver transplantation associated with prolonged ICU stay, increased mortality, and graft loss. Existing risk models focus on donor and surgical variables; the contribution of intraoperative anesthetic management remains poorly characterized in pediatric living donor liver transplantation (LDLT). We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of 124 consecutive pediatric LDLT recipients. Three intraoperative anesthetic parameters were evaluated as predictors of EAD (Olthoff criteria): relative mean arterial pressure (MAP) drop (%), norepinephrine (NE) infusion duration (min), and peak intraoperative lactate (mmol/L). Discriminative performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression addressed near-complete separation. Internal validation used bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations). The cohort (median age 18.5 months, IQR 8.0-96.0; biliary atresia the most common indication) included 50 patients (40.3%) with EAD. All three parameters showed excellent univariable discrimination: NE duration (AUC = 0.993), peak lactate (AUC = 0.936), and MAP drop (AUC = 0.894); all p < 0.001. Three preoperative variables (hemoglobin, bilirubin, albumin) reached univariable significance (all p < 0.05) but with modest discrimination (AUC 0.384-0.617), markedly inferior to all intraoperative parameters (AUC 0.894-0.996). In the multivariable model, MAP drop (OR 22.27; 95% CI 1.80-275.4; p = 0.016) and NE duration (OR 3066657; p = 0.018) independently predicted EAD. The combined model achieved AUC = 0.999 (bootstrap 95% CI: 0.994-1.000; Brier score = 0.013). NE duration ≥ 70 min yielded sensitivity 1.000 and NPV 1.000. EAD-positive patients had significantly longer ICU stay (5 vs. 3 days; p = 0.004) and mechanical ventilation duration (24 vs. 0 h; p < 0.001). Intraoperative anesthetic parameters-particularly NE duration and MAP drop-are powerful independent predictors of EAD in pediatric LDLT, substantially outperforming preoperative variables, three of which reached statistical significance but with markedly lower discriminative power. Intraoperative hemodynamic management may represent a modifiable determinant of early graft outcomes. External validation is warranted.

title: Neurotransmitters and Drug Repurposing in Cancer Therapy: Targeting the Nervous System for Tumor Suppression.
abstract: Emerging research indicates that the nervous system plays a complex role in cancer, with neurotransmitters regulating tumour growth, immune evasion, and resistance to therapy. It has been reported that several important oncogenic pathways are modulated by neurotransmitters, including dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, and glutamate, thereby governing cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and immune regulation in the tumor microenvironment. This has created new opportunities for therapeutic intervention, particularly drug-repurposing strategies that target neurotransmitter signalling. Previous reports have suggested that various neurons can promote the progression of different tumors through neuropeptide receptors, which may represent a potential drug target. Numerous FDA-approved drugs that target neurotransmitter receptors-ranging from dopamine agonists and beta-blockers to Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)-have shown potential anti-cancer activity by modulating tumor-supportive neural signalling. This narrative review synthesizes current literature on the neurobiology of cancer, with an emphasis on the mechanistic roles of dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine/epinephrine in tumorigenesis. It further examines the repurposing of neuroactive drugs-dopamine agonists, SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, and beta- blockers-for cancer therapy, and discusses the more limited evidence on glutamate, acetylcholine, and GABA signalling in tumor biology.

title: Mechanistic Insights into the Neuroprotective Potential of Luteolin: An Overview.
journal: Central nervous system agents in medicinal chemistry
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, are characterized by pathologies such as oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and protein aggregation. Luteolin, a natural flavonoid, is known for its neuroprotective properties, targeting key pathological mechanisms. This review highlights the multi-target effects of luteolin, as demonstrated by in vitro and in vivo studies. Luteolin reduces oxidative damage by scavenging ROS, enhancing antioxidant enzymes, such as SOD, CAT, and GPx, and activating the Nrf2/ARE pathway. It reduces neuroinflammation by inhibiting NF-κB, AP-1, and JNK signalling and by lowering pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-1β. Luteolin maintains mitochondrial membrane potential, modulates apoptotic pathways via Bcl-2/Bax and PI3K/Akt signalling, and promotes autophagy by upregulating LC3-II and modulating the p62-Keap1-Nrf2 axis. It disrupts amyloidogenic and tau hyperphosphorylation pathways, inhibits AChE activity, enhances cholinergic transmission, and improves cognitive function by upregulating CREB, BDNF, and synaptic proteins. Although promising, these effects have been observed mainly in preclinical models, with limited clinical evidence. Future research should focus on the clinical validation and improvement of delivery systems to enhance brain bioavailability. This review provides a foundation for the development of luteolin as a therapeutic candidate for neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Motor-based interventions for brain structure and function in children with developmental coordination disorder: A systematic review.
abstract: To synthesize evidence on the effects of a motor-based intervention on the brain in children with developmental coordination disorder (DCD), and to determine the impact of the different motor-based interventions on the stages of motor learning. For this systematic review, three databases were searched by two independent reviewers. Studies were included if they involved (1) children with (probable) DCD (3-18 years), (2) long-term motor-based interventions, and (3) at least one brain imaging outcome. Two independent reviewers assessed risk of bias (RoB2 and ROBINS-I V2) and evaluated the quality of evidence (GRADE). Seven articles met the selection criteria. Risk of bias ranged from some to moderate (n = 4), to high (n = 3). Various imaging techniques (e.g. functional near-infrared spectroscopy), outcome measures (e.g. oxyhaemoglobin), and regions of interest (e.g. fronto-parietal network) were investigated in the included studies. Despite the neuroplastic changes exhibited by children with DCD post-intervention, the direction and pattern differed from typically developing peers. Increased functional connectivity after intervention was observed in attentional regions, suggesting compensatory mechanisms. The interventions focused on the cognitive (n = 4) and associative (n = 3) stages of motor learning. None of the interventions addressed the autonomous stage. Current evidence tentatively indicates that children with DCD can exhibit intervention-induced neuroplasticity, facilitating motor skill learning. These changes differ from typically developing profiles and therefore seem to reflect compensatory mechanisms. Further research is critical to better understand these differential patterns, essential for interpreting neuroplastic changes to tailor future motor-based therapies.

title: Rising demand, robust triage? Service evaluation of the triage process in a young-onset dementia service.
abstract: To evaluate referrals to our local Young Onset Dementia Assessment Service (YODAS), analyse referral trends and re-referral patterns between 2020 and 2024, and review reasons for non-acceptance of referrals at triage. A retrospective review of electronic referral records was undertaken using descriptive analysis. Referrals to YODAS almost doubled over the study period, while non-acceptance rates remained relatively stable, rising from 52.6% in 2020 to 57.3% in 2024. Among 760 patients whose referrals were not accepted, the most common reasons for non-acceptance were: absence of features suggestive of neurodegeneration, cognitive symptoms better explained by mental health conditions, and insufficient referral information. Over one-quarter were re-referred, with two-thirds subsequently accepted. Only 6% of individuals whose referrals were initially not accepted later received a dementia diagnosis, indicating effective triage. A rise in the demand for dementia assessment from a younger patient population requires a careful triage to ensure the individuals with possible features of neurodegeneration are appropriately assessed, and cases where alternative explanations are more likely are directed to more appropriate pathways.

title: Enhanced observation for management of agitated, confused or distressed behaviours in acute general hospitals: systematic review of quality and safety considerations.
abstract: People who are agitated, confused or distressed seldom receive holistic care within acute general hospitals. Unmet needs relating to conditions such as mental illnesses, learning disabilities or dementia can contribute to patient behaviours which staff find challenging to manage (e.g. self-harm). Enhanced observation, involving one-to-one care and monitoring, is a restrictive intervention often used to manage these presentations. The characteristics and outcomes of high-quality enhanced observation in this setting remain ill-defined, compromising quality and safety. To understand what constitutes high-quality, safe enhanced observation in an acute general hospital for patients presenting with agitated, confused or distressed behaviours. A systematic review was performed, involving searches of five bibliographic databases, hand-searching, and forward and backward citation searching. Data describing the characteristics of high-quality, safe enhanced observation practice were eligible and included in a framework-based synthesis. Quality and safety outcomes were summarised thematically. Studies were appraised for quality, and data interpretation was shaped by lived experience experts. Fifty studies were included. Enhanced observation practice was influenced by individual staff members (e.g. attitudes), teams (e.g. teamwork fluency) and wider organisational factors (e.g. leadership, organisational culture). The quality and safety problems identified included self-harm, aggression and staff neglect of caring responsibilities during enhanced observation. Findings on the characteristics and outcomes of high-quality, safe enhanced observation provision should inform the development of evidence-based guidance to support improved, standardised practice in acute general hospitals. Evidence gaps with respect to patient experiences of enhanced observation and trauma-informed approaches to its delivery warrant urgent attention.

title: Long-term outcomes of daridorexant in those with comorbid insomnia.
abstract: Daridorexant is a dual orexin receptor antagonist recently licensed for chronic insomnia disorder. Guidelines recommend it as a second-line treatment for insomnia, after cognitive-behavioural therapy. Initial trials excluded common comorbidities despite comorbid insomnia being the norm, not the exception. The long-term benefit from daridorexant remains unclear, with few long-term trials. We aimed to assess long-term outcomes in those with comorbid insomnia.This was a retrospective analysis of 38 patients with insomnia who commenced daridorexant. Mental health disorders were common in those referred. Adverse events and a range of insomnia outcomes were assessed. The mean follow-up period was 10.5 months. Of the 38 patients in the study, 95% had comorbid insomnia; 55% experienced benefit from the daridorexant, but 24% discontinued because of side-effects, including vivid dreams, fatigue and worsening anxiety. Three patients experienced worsening mood, one of which included suicidality. Daridorexant can be effective for those with comorbid insomnia, but side-effects may be more common than previously reported.

title: A Dual-Functional Nanoplatform Targeting the dsDNA-cGAS Axis to Mitigate Disc Degeneration and Aberrant Innervation.
abstract: Pathological sensory nerve ingrowth into degenerated intervertebral discs contributes to discogenic pain, yet strategies that concurrently mitigate disc degeneration and pathological innervation remain limited. Here, we found that senescent nucleus pulposus (NP) cells accumulated and released double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), which reinforced NP cell senescence and matrix catabolism. The accumulated dsDNA also activated cGAS-STING signaling, increased Netrin-1 expression, and promoted neuronal migration and neurite outgrowth. Guided by these findings, we developed RU@PEI-ZIF, a dual-functional nanoplatform combining PEI-mediated dsDNA scavenging with ZIF-8-mediated delivery of the cGAS inhibitor RU.521. RU@PEI-ZIF displayed dsDNA-binding capacity, cytocompatibility, and pH-responsive RU.521 release. In senescent NP cells, RU@PEI-ZIF reduced extracellular and cytosolic dsDNA, attenuated cGAS-STING-associated inflammatory and neurotrophic signaling, and reduced NP cell-mediated neuronal migration and neurite outgrowth. In an animal model of disc degeneration, intradiscal RU@PEI-ZIF reduced disc degeneration, NP cell senescence, pathological sensory innervation, and pain hypersensitivity. These findings support RU@PEI-ZIF as a dual-action nanotherapeutic strategy targeting both disc degeneration and pathological innervation.

title: Viroid-Derived siRNAs: Minimal RNAs Driving Multiscale Perturbations of Host Regulatory Systems.
abstract: Viroids are the simplest known infectious agents, consisting of noncoding circular RNAs that replicate autonomously in plant hosts while inducing profound and systemic alterations in host biology. This apparent paradox positions viroids as powerful models for understanding how RNA molecules encode biological information independently of protein translation. A hallmark of viroid infection is the production of viroid-derived small interfering RNAs (vd-siRNAs) by the host RNA silencing machinery. Here, we propose that vd-siRNAs function not merely as antiviroid byproducts, but as active effectors that translate RNA structural information into gene regulatory activity. Through sequence complementarity and selective incorporation into Argonaute complexes, vd-siRNAs influence host gene expression at multiple levels, including transcript abundance, protein accumulation, epigenetic states, and metabolic pathways. Importantly, their effects extend beyond individual targets and are consistent with broader perturbations of interconnected host regulatory networks, potentially contributing to coordinated transcriptional reprogramming and disease-associated phenotypes. By integrating molecular, transcriptomic, epigenetic, and systems-level evidence, we propose a "structure-to-network" perspective in which viroid RNAs function as minimal informational systems capable of interfacing with complex cellular pathways. Within this context, vd-siRNAs emerge as mechanistic links between RNA architecture and multiscale biological responses. Finally, we discuss how this framework expands our understanding of RNA-mediated regulation and highlights the broader regulatory potential of structured noncoding RNAs.

title: Vascular profiling of the spinal cord and cortex reveals region-specific endothelial dysfunction and fibroblast remodeling in human ALS.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons. Increasing evidence suggests that neurovascular dysfunction contributes to ALS pathogenesis, but a comprehensive understanding of vascular cell alterations in the human central nervous system remains lacking. Here, to systematically characterize neurovascular changes in ALS, we curated single-nucleus transcriptomic datasets from human spinal cord and cortical tissues with a specific focus on vascular cell populations. Comparative analyses revealed substantial vascular perturbations in the spinal cord compared to the cortex. Among vascular-associated cell populations, endothelial cells and fibroblasts exhibited the most pronounced transcriptional alterations. Endothelial cells from ALS spinal cords displayed reduced blood-brain barrier integrity signatures and increased expression of inflammatory and stress-response programs, with the greatest changes manifested in capillary endothelial cells. In parallel, we generated a refined cellular atlas of spinal cord fibroblasts and identified three major fibroblast populations, including a distinct LAMA1low perivascular fibroblast subtype. Fibroblast signatures were found to be consistently elevated in ALS across single-nucleus transcriptomic, bulk transcriptomic, and experimental validation datasets. Together, our findings establish a region-resolved view of neurovascular alternations in human ALS, which is characterized by endothelial barrier dysfunction and disease-associated remodeling of specialized perivascular fibroblasts. These findings broaden the cellular framework of ALS pathogenesis beyond neuronal and glial alterations and highlight the neurovascular niche as an integral component of human ALS disease biology.

title: Impact of environmental enrichment and allostatic load induced by repeated mixing on the transcriptome of three porcine brain tissues.
abstract: Environmental enrichment and mixing represent two management procedures in pig production with opposing effects: while environmental enrichment can promote welfare by reducing stress, repeated mixing often induces stress and can negatively impact welfare. Despite their importance in pig husbandry, how these opposing management procedures affect brain function at the molecular level remains poorly understood. This study investigated how environmental enrichment and allostatic load induced by repeated mixing influence gene expression patterns across three porcine brain regions: hypothalamus, prefrontal cortex, and hippocampus. Using RNA sequencing, we analyzed brain tissues from 48 gilts subjected to a 2 × 2 factorial design comparing enrichment conditions (enriched vs. barren) and allostatic load (repeated vs. minimal mixing). While environmental enrichment showed minimal impact on gene expression, allostatic load resulted in 38 differentially expressed genes in the hippocampus, primarily involved in hormone regulation, protein transport, and neuronal activity. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) identified modules moderately correlated with experimental conditions: six modules in hippocampus associated with allostatic load, and four modules in hypothalamus associated with enrichment. Functional annotation revealed that these modules were primarily enriched in biological processes related to synaptic signaling, neuron development, and metabolic activity. Hub genes from these modules were identified, and turned out not to overlap with differentially expressed genes. Our findings suggest that based on this experimental design, the hippocampus may be particularly responsive to stress-induced transcriptomic changes, while the molecular effects of the environmental enrichment appear more subtle. Overall, this study reveals limited but region-specific transcriptional responses to allostatic load in the porcine brain.

title: Brain imaging-derived phenotypes influence risk of bipolar disorder: comprehensive exposome-wide association and wide-angled genetic analyses.
abstract: Despite many reported imaging markers for bipolar disorder (BD), systematic assessment across diverse brain imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) is lacking. We used epidemiological and genetic analyses to progress from association to causality and identify candidate biomarkers and potential pathways of BD. We conducted an Exposome-Wide Association Study (ExWAS) in 35,680 UK Biobank participants to assess associations of 686 brain IDPs with BD. Genetic correlations were estimated via linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC). Bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) and meta-analysis were performed using large-scale GWAS data to infer causality. Additional analyses, including Functional Mapping and Annotation (FUMA), protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, and spatiotemporal gene expression profiling during human brain development, were performed to investigate potential biological mechanisms of BD and IDPs. In our ExWAS analyses, we identified 10 significant exposome-level IDPs, and LDSC further revealed 67 IDPs with significant genetic correlations with BD. The MR analyses provided robust causal evidence for 12 IDPs, 6 of which were further validated by meta-analysis. Integrative analyses identified two associations supported by both epidemiological and genetic evidence (IDP.1510: fractional anisotropy in the forceps major, and IDP.0387: volume of the right lateral orbital frontal cortex). Additionally, we identified pleiotropic genes between IDPs and BD. Gene enrichment analyses implicated shared biological pathways, such as nucleosome assembly and neutrophil extracellular trap formation . PPI network analysis suggested that histone family members occupied central hubs in the interaction network. Spatiotemporal expression profiling identified region-specific developmental trajectories of pleiotropic genes in brain regions, including the cerebellum and thalamus, with the late fetal to early postnatal period potentially representing a sensitive developmental period for neurodevelopmental effects of BD susceptibility genes. This study establishes an atlas of brain IDPs associated with BD, by integrating epidemiological and genetic evidence. The findings highlight candidate IDPs, including right lateral orbital frontal cortex volume and fractional anisotropy in the forceps major, that were consistently associated with BD across complementary analyses. Our results provide genetically supported targets for early intervention and precision psychiatry.

title: Evaluating the effects of metronidazole, metformin, and onion extract on GAPDH activity and nitric oxide production in Blastocystis sp. cultures: a biochemical and therapeutic approach.
abstract: Blastocystis sp. is a highly prevalent anaerobic intestinal protozoan increasingly associated with gastrointestinal disorders. Its survival within the gut microenvironment depends on metabolic pathways such as glycolysis, where glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) plays a central role, alongside interactions with nitric oxide (NO) derived from host defenses and surrounding microbiota. The emergence of metronidazole resistance necessitates exploration of alternative therapeutic strategies. To evaluate the in vitro effects of metronidazole, metformin, and Allium cepa (onion) extract on Blastocystis sp. growth, and GAPDH activity and NO levels within the xenic culture medium. Twenty-one Blastocystis-positive stool samples were cultured in Jones' medium under xenic conditions. Cultures were treated with graded concentrations of metronidazole, metformin, and onion extract. Parasite counts were assessed microscopically, while GAPDH activity and NO levels were quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS)-based analysis. All tested agents significantly reduced Blastocystis counts compared with untreated controls (p < 0.05), with metronidazole demonstrating the greatest antiparasitic effect. Significant reductions in NO levels and GAPDH activity were observed across all treatment groups (p < 0.001). Metformin (1000 µg/mL) showed the strongest inhibition of GAPDH activity, whereas metronidazole (500 µg/mL) resulted in the lowest NO levels. Correlation analysis revealed a significant negative association between NO and GAPDH in metronidazole-treated cultures, while a positive correlation was observed with metformin. Metronidazole, metformin, and onion extract exhibit significant anti-Blastocystis activity, accompanied by modulation of key metabolic and nitrosative pathways within the microbial milieu supporting the growth of Blastocystis sp. Targeting GAPDH and NO-related mechanisms represents a promising therapeutic approach, particularly in the context of emerging drug resistance and co-colonization with other gut microbiota.

title: The effectiveness of guided botulinum toxin "A" injection to the masticatory muscles in the management of condylar and sub condylar fractures: a randomized controlled clinical trial.
abstract: To evaluate the effectiveness of ultrasound guided injection of botulinum toxin A into the muscles of mastication; the masseter, temporalis and the lateral pterygoid, in a closed reduction approach of condylar and sub-condylar fractures, to optimize fracture reduction, reduce the length of intermaxillary fixation (IMF) and to facilitate postoperative functional recovery. Sixteen medically healthy patients aged 18-35 years, presenting with unilateral subcondylar fracture were randomly assigned into two groups. The randomized controlled clinical trial was completed after recruitment, intervention, and follow up of all participants. The Study group (A) underwent an intervention involving ultrasound-guided Botulinum Toxin (BTX) injection into the Lateral Pterygoid Muscle (LPM), the Temporalis and the Masseter muscles, followed by the closed reduction treatment of the fracture, compared to the control group (B) that underwent conventional treatment method; the closed reduction approach without any BTX injections. Pain scores were significantly lower in the study group (A), especially after the botulinum toxin injection (p < 0.001*) which subsequently led to a significantly shorter operation time (p < 0.001*) in the study group compared with the control group (B). Following surgery, mouth opening improved significantly over time in both groups (p < 0.001*); however, the study group showed significantly greater improvement at 14 days (31.44 ± 2.72 mm versus 14.46 ± 3.24 mm, in the control group; p < 0.001*) and at 6 weeks postoperatively, (38.02 ± 3.26 mm versus 17.88 ± 4.49 mm; p < 0.001*) respectively. Regarding structural outcomes, patients in the study group demonstrated significantly better postoperative reduction accuracy, with lower angulation values (p < 0.02*) immediately postoperative and at 6 months compared with the control group. Finally, bone density at the fracture line increased significantly over time in both groups (p < 0.001*), however no significant difference was noted comparing both groups together (p = 0.37). The addition of guided botulinum toxin A to the closed reduction protocols for subcondylar fractures significantly reduces postoperative pain and operative duration while optimizing alignment accuracy and functional mobility recovery. Given that bone healing remains uncompromised, this approach serves as an efficient, reliable alternative that directly improves patient outcomes. Completed. The study was initially designed and ethically approved as an institutional clinical investigation. Trial registration was subsequently undertaken upon recognition of the importance of public trial registration in promoting transparency and facilitating dissemination of the study findings. The study protocol, eligibility criteria, outcome measures, and statistical analysis plan were defined prior to patient enrollment and remained unchanged following registration. The study was retrospectively registered with ClinicalTrials.gov on January 28, 2026 (NCT07374341).

title: The effects of universal parental support programs: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: There are few current comprehensive meta-analyses and systematic reviews of the literature on universal parental support programs. The aim of this meta-analysis was therefore to examine the effects of universal parental support programs on children's externalizing and internalizing problems, as well as on parental mental health, and to evaluate the possible importance of theoretical frameworks in achieving better outcomes. The meta-analysis included randomized controlled trials of universal parental support programs for parents to children and adolescents aged 2-17 years. A search in five databases was conducted from inception to December 2020 and updated in April 2024. The abstracts and subsequent full-text articles were independently reviewed by two pairs of authors, resulting in 31 original studies (36 articles) with a total of 7635 participants. To evaluate risk of bias, we used the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials. Small positive short-term effects were obtained for the included universal parental support programs on parental ratings of children's externalizing (d = 0.18: 95% CI 0.07-0.29) and internalizing problems (d = 0.16: 95% CI 0.03-0.30), parental stress (d = 0.22: 95% CI 0.04-0.40) and parental depression (d = 0.13: 95% CI 0.01-0.25). Subgroup analyses showed that significant effects on primary outcomes were only found when interventions were compared to waitlist, not to an active control group. The long-term between-group effects were positive but small and non-significant. Most of the programs were based on social learning theory, no differences emerged between programs with different theoretical frameworks. This meta-analysis indicates that universal parental support programs, when compared to waitlist only, may have a small positive impact on children's externalizing and internalizing problems as well as on parental stress and depression in the short time frame.

title: Magnesium sulfate versus dexmedetomidine as adjuvants for peribulbar block: a GRADE-assessed systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Regional anesthesia is widely used for ophthalmic surgery, but peribulbar block may have slower onset and variable akinesia. Dexmedetomidine and magnesium sulfate are used as adjuvants, yet their comparative effects remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA 2020 and Cochrane guidance (PROSPERO CRD420261435378). PubMed, Embase, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Cochrane and Google Scholar were searched from inception to May 2026 for randomized controlled trials comparing magnesium sulfate with dexmedetomidine as adjuvants to peribulbar local anesthetic. Random-effects meta-analysis used REML, conventional and Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals, prediction intervals, leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, dosage and surgery-based subgroup analyses, and GRADE assessment. Six randomized controlled trials were included. Most pooled outcomes showed no statistically significant between-group differences, including sensory-block onset (MD - 0.04 min, 95% CI - 0.15 to 0.06), globe-akinesia onset (MD - 0.33 min, 95% CI - 1.61 to 0.96), globe-akinesia duration (MD - 11.46 min, 95% CI - 29.68 to 6.77), time to block adequacy (MD 0.10 min, 95% CI - 0.92 to 1.12), IOP at 5 and 10 min, akinesia scores, supplementary injection, and satisfaction. Dexmedetomidine was associated with faster lid-akinesia onset in the conventional analysis (MD 0.32 min, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.50; P = 0.0003), but the HK-adjusted CI crossed the null (- 0.31 to 0.95). Conventional analyses also favored dexmedetomidine for lid-akinesia duration (MD - 12.20 min, P = 0.0188) and time to first analgesia (MD - 18.22 min, P = 0.0101), but both lost statistical significance after HK adjustment. Heterogeneity was substantial for several outcomes, and GRADE certainty ranged from high to very low, with most outcomes rated very low. Current evidence does not establish a clear efficacy or safety advantage of magnesium sulfate or dexmedetomidine as a peribulbar adjuvant. Apparent benefits for lid-akinesia onset, lid-akinesia duration, and time to first analgesia are sensitive to conservative statistical adjustment and should not be interpreted as definitive. The evidence base is small, heterogeneous, geographically concentrated, and generally low or very low certainty; adequately powered multicenter trials with standardized dosing and outcome assessment are needed.

title: Pediatric Large Cell/Anaplastic Medulloblastomas: Diagnostic Concordance and Multi-Classifier DNA Methylation Profiling, Including the In-House MAGIBU Framework.
journal: Neuropathology : official journal of the Japanese Society of Neuropathology
abstract: Large cell/anaplastic medulloblastoma is a high-risk variant whose histopathological diagnosis can be challenging. We analyzed 12 pediatric cases enriched for LC/A morphology, with centralized review available for 11. In this deliberately selected, diagnostically challenging series, institutional and central LC/A versus non-LC/A assessments were discordant in 36% (4 of 11), illustrating the difficulty of applying the LC/A designation rather than a general estimate of inter-observer reproducibility. DNA methylation profiling was performed using four classifiers: Heidelberg CNS Tumor Methylation Classifier, Methylscape Analysis, EpiDiP, and the MAGIBU classifier, which applies a UMAP-based distance approach. Tumor classification was largely concordant across platforms, identifying two WNT-activated medulloblastomas, eight non-WNT/non-SHH medulloblastomas, and one tumor reclassified as an embryonal tumor with multilayered rosettes. One misclassification occurred with EpiDiP, where an SHH-activated medulloblastoma aligned with the normal cerebellar cortex reference profile. Copy number analysis revealed MYC amplification in two non-WNT/non-SHH tumors, chromosome 6 loss in both WNT-activated cases, and isochromosome 17q in one MYC-amplified non-WNT/non-SHH tumor. Adjunctive molecular data for a subset of cases were obtained from PedcBioPortal. The reclassified tumor lacked canonical molecular alterations but harbored additional CTNNB1 and TP53 variants whose contribution to its pathogenesis remains uncertain. One WNT-activated medulloblastoma also carried a CTNNB1 variant. The MAGIBU classifier correctly identified the ETMR case, classified all remaining tumors as medulloblastomas, and showed concordant subgroup assignment with the Heidelberg CNS Tumor Methylation Classifier and Methylscape Analysis, including the SHH-activated case misclassified by EpiDiP. On external validation across four independent medulloblastoma cohorts (n = 1063), MAGIBU achieved 98.5% family-level recall and 96.4% subclass-level recall. In conclusion, our findings indicate that, in these diagnostically challenging, LC/A-enriched cases, morphology-based diagnostic assessment can be inconsistent. DNA methylation profiling serves to refine tumor reclassification and ensure accurate risk stratification. Interpreting each tumor across complementary classifiers provides a triangulation that enhances diagnostic robustness.

title: Ayahuasca Impairs Fear Memory Reconsolidation and Promotes Rapid Structural Plasticity in the Hippocampus and Prelimbic Cortex.
abstract: Psychedelic drugs promote rapid neuroplasticity in brain regions affected by trauma exposure, such as the prelimbic (PL) cortex and the dorsal hippocampus (DH), being investigated as potential treatments for posttraumatic stress disorder. Ayahuasca (Aya) contains N,N-dimethyltryptamine, a classic psychedelic. Our previous work showed that Aya reduces fear expression by impairing fear memory reconsolidation. We hypothesized that Aya administration during reconsolidation induces neuroplastic changes in DH and PL cortex associated with its behavioral effects. Adult male Wistar rats underwent contextual fear conditioning and received Aya (60 mg/kg, oral gavage) or H₂O (vehicle) 20 min before or 3 h after fear memory retrieval. To confirm the reconsolidation-impairing effect of Aya, animals were re-exposed to the conditioned context 24 h later. Structural plasticity was assessed 24 h after retrieval and drug administration by Golgi-Cox staining of the DH and the PL cortex. Neurogenesis was evaluated 10 days later by doublecortin (DCX) immunohistochemistry of dentate gyrus. Aya significantly reduced freezing behavior, confirming the reconsolidation-impairing effect. This outcome was accompanied by increased dendritic spine density in the CA1, CA3, and dentate gyrus regions of the DH, as well as in the PL cortex. In the PL cortex, Aya altered dendritic branching and length depending on the timing of administration. In contrast, Aya did not affect adult hippocampal neurogenesis. Together, these findings suggest that rapid synaptic remodeling in the DH and PL cortex, rather than changes in adult hippocampal neurogenesis, is associated with the reconsolidation-impairing effect of Aya.

title: Cyclophilin D deficiency exacerbates diet-induced obesity and selectively enhances skeletal muscle mitochondrial respiration in male mice.
journal: Pflugers Archiv : European journal of physiology
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of obesity-associated metabolic disease, with the mitochondrial permeability transition pore serving as a key regulator of cellular energy homeostasis. Cyclophilin D, encoded by Ppif, is the principal regulatory component of this pore and has been implicated in insulin secretion, adipocyte survival, and whole-body energy balance. However, whether Ppif loss produces a consistent metabolic phenotype when challenged with high fat diet (HFD) exposure, and whether systemic metabolic alterations reflect tissue-specific changes in mitochondrial oxidative capacity, remains unresolved. Here, we characterized male, 21-weeks-old mice with germline Ppif deletion longitudinally over 34 weeks under standard (SD) and HFD using body composition analysis, indirect calorimetry, glucose and insulin tolerance testing and tissue-resolved, Seahorse-based mitochondrial respirometry. Under SD, knockout mice displayed elevated fat mass without differences in food intake or energy expenditure. High-fat feeding progressively amplified this adiposity, with knockout mice developing significantly greater body weight and fat mass than wild-type littermates by weeks 28 and 36. Glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity remained comparable between genotypes under either diet. ANCOVA revealed significant effects of lean mass (p < 0.001) and genotype (p = 0.017) on energy expenditure, as well as a significant lean mass × genotype interaction (p = 0.025). Consistent with a distinct contribution of lean mass to EE in KO vs. WT mice, we found increased ADP-stimulated mitochondrial respiration in quadriceps of knockout mice under both diets, without corresponding differences in brown adipose tissue or liver, or changes in mitochondrial content across tissues. These findings establish cyclophilin D as a diet- and tissue-specific regulator of energy homeostasis, informing therapeutic strategies targeting the permeability transition pore or cyclophilin D interactome in metabolic disease.

title: Acute Ischaemic Stroke: Therapeutic Targets and Key Modulators of the Fibrinolytic System and Clot Formation.
abstract: The processes of clot formation and clot dissolution with fibrinolysis underpin the pathophysiological mechanisms of acute ischaemic stroke (AIS) and its treatment. Detailed understanding of the modulation of this system is required to develop effective and safe stroke therapeutics. Clot formation occurs with the interaction of the coagulation cascade, along with platelets and fibrin meshwork. Conversely, fibrinolysis involves the serine protease plasmin, its zymogen, plasminogen and its enzymatic conversion by tissue plasminogen activator. The regulators and inhibitors that modulate the interactions in clot formation and fibrinolysis can be potential targets for new and emerging stroke therapies. The aim of this narrative review is to help inform stroke clinicians and researchers about the role of the fibrinolytic system and its inhibitors in AIS and the potential for new therapeutic targets. We outline the processes involved in clot formation and dissolution, the role of endogenous inhibitors of the fibrinolytic system, followed by potential therapeutic targets including tissue plasminogen activators as well as novel therapies and adjuncts. Better understanding of these processes will provide insight into the variable response to current stroke fibrinolytics amongst AIS patients and help to develop new and improved AIS therapeutics in future.

title: Beyond Weight Loss: Facial Remodeling Associated with GLP-1 Receptor Agonists-A Systematic Review and Therapeutic Framework.
abstract: Facial volume depletion and skin laxity have increasingly been reported during weight loss associated with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) treatment. However, these changes are not recognized as a distinct clinical entity and may overlap with those occurring after other forms of rapid or massive weight loss. Evidence regarding their treatment remains limited. This systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261415797). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception to June 5, 2026. Clinical studies evaluating interventions for facial changes associated with GLP-1RA-related weight loss were included. Study characteristics, interventions, outcomes, safety, and methodological limitations were synthesized narratively. Risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools. Four uncontrolled observational studies involving 98 treated participants met the eligibility criteria. Two studies enrolled exclusively patients receiving GLP-1RAs or related incretin-based medications, whereas two included mixed weight-loss etiologies. Investigated interventions included injectable biostimulators and fillers, endotissutal bipolar radiofrequency, and a topical formulation. All studies reported favorable within-group findings; however, heterogeneous populations, weight-loss trajectories, interventions, outcomes, and follow-up durations, together with the absence of comparator groups, precluded conclusions regarding treatment effectiveness or superiority. The available evidence is preliminary and insufficient to support a validated therapeutic algorithm. The proposed framework is hypothesis-generating and integrates limited review findings with established principles of post-weight-loss facial rejuvenation. Comparative studies evaluating surgical and nonsurgical interventions are required. This journal requires that authors assign a level of evidence to each article. For a full description of these Evidence-Based Medicine ratings, please refer to the Table of Contents or the online Instructions to Authors www.springer.com/00266 . Trial registration number PROSPERO Registration CRD420261415797.

title: Cystatin C and its Role in the Neuro-Glial-Vascular Unit: Implications for Cerebrovascular Diseases and Neurodegeneration.
abstract: Cystatin C (CysC) is emerging as a key regulator and intercellular signaling mediator within the neuro-glial-vascular unit (NGVU). This review comprehensively examines its multifaceted roles across NGVU components, detailing mechanisms by which CysC preserves blood-brain barrier integrity, modulates neuroinflammation, and influences pathological protein aggregation. Rather than providing a merely descriptive catalogue, we emphasize its context-dependent nature. In cerebrovascular and neurodegenerative diseases, CysC exhibits functional duality along the neuron-glia axis, either restraining or perpetuating inflammation and proteinopathy depending on cellular context and disease stage. Similarly, along the endothelial-oligodendrocyte precursor cell crosstalk, its coordination of angiogenesis and myelination may shift from protective to detrimental under chronic hypoperfusion. We evaluate its dual utility as a clinical biomarker and therapeutic target, addressing challenges in brain delivery, target selectivity, and safety. This integrative synthesis provides a critical perspective on unresolved controversies and future research priorities regarding CysC in neurological disorders.
